preamble: Long [uː] diphthongizing to [au] (via [ʊu]/[əu]) is the back half of the paired diphthongization of the long high vowels found in English and High German, matched by [iː] > [ai] in the front. English did it in the Great Vowel Shift (hūs > house). High German did it independently in the New High German diphthongization, which started in Upper Bavarian in the 12th century and reached Moselle Franconian only in the 16th. Northern English and Scots, Alemannic and Ripuarian keep the old monophthong (Scots hoose, Swiss German Huus).
phoneticEffects: Diphthongization, Great Vowel Shift, New High German Diphthongization

examples.note: Great Vowel Shift (c. 1400–1700). ME /uː/ went through [ʊu]/[əu] to modern [aʊ]. Northern English and Scots, where ME /uː/ survived, did not undergo it.

New High German diphthongization of MHG ī, ū, iu to ei, au, eu (snîden > schneiden, liute > Leute). It started in Upper Bavarian in the 12th century and spread north and west. Alemannic (except Swabian) and Ripuarian keep [uː].
